title: The creeper (334–337)
hookLine: craving grows like a creeper in a careless person; he leaps like a monkey from tree to tree

lines: A THREAD ON THE FENCE IN JUNE.
cards: If you've ever left a garden alone for one summer, you know what a vine can do. In June it's a little green thread on the fence. By August it has climbed the fence, swallowed a bush, and started up the side of the house.
Nobody planted it there on purpose. It just grew, a little every day, while no one was looking. A new chapter of the book begins today, twenty-six verses long, and it opens with that vine.

teach.b: The chapter's name, and today's word, is tanha: thirst. In Buddhist teaching it's craving, the restless wanting that the second noble truth calls the cause of suffering.
You met it in the Buddha's first sermon; now the Dhammapada gives it pictures.

Verse three hundred thirty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest." Two pictures in one verse.
The creeper grows slowly, quietly, wrapping itself around whatever it touches. The monkey leaps from branch to branch, grabbing one fruit, dropping it, reaching for the next.

That's craving from outside and from inside: it spreads, and it never sits still. The next verses say what happens either way. For the one overcome by this thirst, sorrows grow like wild grass after rain.

teach.h: WILD GRASS, OR DROPS OFF A LOTUS LEAF.
teach.b: For the one who overcomes it, sorrows fall away like drops of water from a lotus leaf.

teach.h: IT GROWS WHERE NO ONE WATCHES.
teach.b: Notice the word thoughtless, or careless. It's the book's old theme from chapter two, heedfulness. The vine doesn't win by force.
It wins because nobody's watching the fence.
So the first step with tanha isn't to fight it. It's to notice it early, while it's still a thread.
Teachers describe three kinds: craving for pleasant things, craving to become something, and craving to be rid of something. All three climb the same way, a little every day.

how: Buddhists across traditions name tanha, craving, as the cause of suffering in the second noble truth; meditators practice noticing craving as it arises, often with a quiet mental label.

o: craving: a restless thirst that keeps on growing
a feeling of sadness after losing something
any healthy desire, like hunger or ambition

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: sorrows falling from the one who's free

s: Müller named the whole chapter 'thirst'; in teaching it means craving.
the verse says craving wins by force
it grows in a careless person, while no one watches the fence.
Buddhist teachers describe three kinds of craving
for pleasant things, for becoming, and for being rid of something.

games.q: you notice the first thread of a craving: a small urge to check your phone. what does today's teaching suggest first?
o: notice it early, while it's still a thread.
ignore it; it's too small to matter.
games.why: the creeper grows in the careless; the first step is to see it early, before it has climbed the house.

practice: Rest with the breath and watch, quietly, for the first thread of a wanting: to shift position, to check the time, for this to be over, for a snack later.
When one appears, name it silently, thirst, and neither pull it out nor follow it; just see what happens when you simply see it. Then back to the breath, until the next thread.

wordCard.voice: Tanha. Thirst, craving: the wanting that grows like a creeper and leaps like a monkey.

orig.note: Pali taṇhā (Sanskrit tṛṣṇā): thirst, craving; the name of chapter twenty-four.

carryVoice: Your line: the creeper grows. Seen early, it's only a thread. Day two hundred eighteen.
